draft.title: Steam power and factories
card: A steam engine burns fuel, usually coal, to boil water. The steam pushes parts of the engine and makes them move.
Early steam engines wasted a lot of fuel. James Watt made them far more efficient in the 1760s and 1770s, so they became cheap enough for many businesses to use.
Steam engines could drive machines anywhere, not just beside a river. Owners built factories in towns and filled them with machines, especially for making cotton cloth.
Steam power later moved people and goods. Steam trains ran on railways and steamships crossed oceans.
draft.remember: Better steam engines gave factories a power source that did not depend on rivers.

a.q: Why did James Watt's improvements to the steam engine matter for industry?
opts: They made engines efficient enough for many factories to use
They made engines that needed no fuel to work
They let factories run only by rivers and streams
They replaced machines with workers who made cloth by hand
a.why: Watt's engines used fuel more efficiently, so more businesses could afford them to power machines. Engines still needed fuel, and the card says steam power freed factories from rivers.
a.clue: Think about what made engines cheap enough to spread.

b.q: In 1800, Tom owns a cotton mill. His old mill was beside a river and used a water wheel. He wants to build a new mill in the middle of a town. What makes this possible?
opts: A steam engine can power machines away from a river
A water wheel works better in a town than by a river
Cotton can only be spun in towns
Steamships can carry the mill's cloth to the town
b.why: A steam engine burns coal to make power, so it can run machines wherever the coal can be taken. A water wheel needs moving water, so it does not suit a town. Steamships were a later use of steam power and do not decide where a mill is built.
b.clue: What did a steam engine need that a water wheel needed in a river?

a.best: They made engines efficient enough for many factories to use

b.best: A steam engine can power machines away from a river

problems.detail: The clue 'What did a steam engine need that a water wheel needed in a river?' is garbled and confusing. It seems to mean 'What did a water wheel need that a steam engine did not?' and should be reworded.

Dating Watt's improvements to 'the 1760s and 1770s' leaves out the 1780s. His rotary-motion engines (from about 1781–82), which let steam drive factory machines directly, came then. It would be more accurate to say 'from the 1760s to the 1780s'.
